newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: Seoul move to aid banks sends right signal - analyst.
newsitem.headline: Seoul move to aid banks sends right signal - analyst.

text.p: South Korea's decision to break its long silence on its banking sector woes and to consider giving loans to merchant banks would send the right signal to the international financial community, analysts said on Thursday.
The Finance Ministry said a number of measures were being considered to rescue Korea First Bank, a leading commercial bank that was the hardest hit by a chain of loan defaults by big conglomerates.
The Bank of Korea had supplied $1.0 billion in emergency loans on Tuesday to seven commercial banks to ease dollar shortages.
"The government wants to raise banks' overseas credit ratings, and I believe the move will pay off," said Kim Chul-beom, banking analyst at ABN Amro Hoare Govett Asia.

Finance ministry spokesman Chung Eui-dong said the government was concerned about plans by rating agencies Standard & Poor's Corp (S&P) and Moody's Investors Service to downgrade the credit rating of some South Korean banks.

"We are passing through the worst phase of banking difficulties with the government's intervention. But it will take a time to turn around," said Scott Seo, banking analyst at Deutsche Morgan Grenfell Capital Markets Ltd.
"When the government sends a strong signal that as big brother, it will not stand idly by, the attitude of the overseas financial industry towards Korean banks will stabilise."
The government gave no details on its plans.

Analysts and South Korean newspapers said the government was thinking of extending special central bank loans or allowing Korea First Bank to raise its capital by offering a rights issue which the government would undertake.
Korea First Bank had already requested three trillion won ($3.35 billion) in special loans from the central bank. But the Bank of Korea had not responded yet.
Another step under review was to change the rule that requires banks to set aside reserves equivalent to 90 percent of their non-performing loans.
This rule has become increasingly burdensome for South Korea's struggling banks.
The government's announcement came after officials from Moody's and S&P visited the finance ministry to discuss prospects for the country's economy and whether or not the government would help banks.
"We believe our move will contribute to the rating agencies having a positive outlook," said a finance ministry official. "Except for Korea First Bank, other banks are in good shape."
Interest rate spreads have been widening for all South Korean banks due to the deteriorating financial condition of the country's corporate and banking sectors.

S&P, placing five South Korean banks on its watch list, said it might cut their ratings further. Analysts said Korea First would suffer most as it was heavily exposed to the financially troubled the Jinro, Hanbo, Sammi and Kia groups.

A Korea First official said the bank was now delaying most overseas borrowing plans, as interest rates for the bank recently shot up to 0.6-0.7 percentage point over the London Interbank Offered Rate (LIBOR) from 0.2-0.3 a year earlier.
The bank's long-term debt is currently rated BBB-minus by S&P, down from BBB-plus in April.
If the rating agency were to downgrade Korea First Bank another notch, the bank would become speculative grade and it would be unable to issue any long-term bonds overseas.
An official at the Industrial Bank of Korea said it was unable to sell $250 million in corporate papers abroad since the rating agencies announced it might cut the bank's ratings.
"Many foreign investors sat tight on the sidelines as our products are regarded as already downgraded by rating agencies," he said. "Government help is essential." (Conversion $1 = 894.30 won)
